summary: The Clergy Act lets ordained ministers, religious order members, and Christian Science practitioners who previously opted out of Social Security revoke that exemption by filing an IRS application no later than their 2030 tax return due date, with the revocation taking effect for 2029 or 2030 and all later years, and requires payment of any back taxes if the filing is late for the chosen year.

scores.thoughts: The bill permits clergy to voluntarily opt into Social Security coverage, which could result in marginally higher future benefit outlays from the Social Security trust funds. This represents a very minor expansion of participation in an entitlement program rather than any direct appropriation or spending increase by Congress. The effect is tangential at best.

By allowing revocation of the existing exemption, the bill creates an optional pathway for clergy to begin paying Social Security payroll taxes. No tax rates are changed and participation remains voluntary, so any revenue impact is both small and elective.
The bill addresses only Social Security coverage elections for clergy and contains no provisions related to health insurance, Medicare, Medicaid, or healthcare delivery systems.
No provisions address firearms, background checks, or gun regulations of any kind.
The legislation is silent on immigration policy, visas, border enforcement, or pathways to citizenship.
No language pertains to reproductive rights, abortion access, or funding restrictions.
The bill does not alter defense authorizations, military spending levels, or veterans' benefits outside the general Social Security framework.
No environmental, energy, or regulatory provisions are present.

Social Security is a core component of the social safety net. The bill expands the pool of potential participants by giving previously exempt clergy a time-limited opportunity to opt in, thereby slightly broadening coverage and future benefit eligibility for that group.
The measure contains nothing related to schools, student aid, or education policy.
No references to controlled substances, decriminalization, or enforcement appear in the text.
The bill does not address sentencing, policing, incarceration, or criminal justice reform.
No trade, tariff, or globalization provisions are included.
Any fiscal effect would be limited to the self-financed Social Security system and would not directly affect general-fund deficits or debt-reduction strategies.
The legislation makes no mention of sexual orientation, gender identity, or related civil rights protections.
Foreign assistance programs are unaffected by this domestic Social Security election change.
No election administration, voting access, or campaign finance provisions exist.
The bill does not regulate technology companies, data collection, or privacy standards.
Nothing in the text addresses collective bargaining, union rights, or workplace labor standards.

The bill modifies an existing religious exemption from Social Security by giving clergy a one-time window to revoke that exemption. It neither strengthens nor curtails religious accommodations; it merely provides an optional administrative pathway to end a prior election.
